digest.definition: Chemistry is the central science, describing, explaining and changing the material world, with large effects on society and a key part in sustainable development and global challenges
distinctiveFeatures: Chemistry is the central science, describing, explaining and changing the material world, with large effects on society and a key part in sustainable development and global challenges

A very broad discipline, organised in many ways: the traditional inorganic, organic, physical and analytical branches; synthesis, measurement and application; or applied fields such as biological, computational, environmental, materials or medicinal chemistry
Hands-on practical work is essential, built up in a spiral from scripted experiments to independent, precise work by the final year
Theory is underpinned by mathematical, spatial, information, planning, communication and problem-solving skills; the subject has a strong visual and practical side
An inherently creative, multidisciplinary subject whose graduates combine subject expertise with wider attributes valued by employers in and beyond science

Two undergraduate routes, the bachelor's with honours and the integrated master's (MChem, MSci), plus standalone MSc and MRes courses; accreditation by the Royal Society of Chemistry towards Chartered Chemist

subjectSpecific.text: By the end of your course you should be able to describe and discuss the key concepts across the whole of chemistry with confidence, accuracy and detail, in the right terms.
By the end of your course you should be able to describe, record and follow safe practice, managing toxicity, stability and reactivity through knowledge-led risk assessment and practical work.
By the end of your course you should be able to cut waste in practical work and use disposal methods that protect people in the laboratory and the environment.

By the end of your course you should be able to explain and justify how thermodynamics (classical and statistical), kinetics, quantum mechanics and spectroscopy work, and use them on problems in theory and in the laboratory.

By the end of your course you should be able to predict likely products, bond-forming reactions, mechanisms, stereochemistry and reactivity, and use those predictions to propose routes to target compounds and to design experiments that test them.

By the end of your course you should be able to explain, plan and use ways to purify, isolate and characterise substances, guided by the physical and chemical properties and periodic trends of the elements and their compounds.

By the end of your course you should be able to discuss trends across the periodic table, explain what they mean for how elements react and behave and for their physical properties, and use this on problems in theory and practice.
By the end of your course you should be able to describe atomic and molecular orbitals and how they help explain structure, bonding and the paths reactions take.

By the end of your course you should be able to plan, develop and carry out qualitative and quantitative preparation and purification of samples, measurement, metrology and analysis, attending to accuracy, precision, traceability, complex matrices and sample size.

By the end of your course you should be able to explain the theory behind classical and instrumental analytical techniques and their limits, carry out analyses and measurements and report them in the right terms and notation.
By the end of your course you should be able to use computational methods and software to understand chemical structure, bonding and reactivity better.
By the end of your course you should be able to know many organic and inorganic compounds, substances and materials and what each is for.
By the end of your course you should be able to recognise how chemistry has fed the innovations of the modern world and how chemists can help meet present and future challenges.
By the end of your course you should be able to see how chemistry relates to and meets other subjects, so as to work well in multidisciplinary settings.
Your course may also give you the chance to think about and discuss where and how chemistry grew as a culture and what it has done to society.
Your course may also give you the chance to focus on one or more specialist branches, for example sustainable (green) chemistry, cheminformatics or the teaching of chemistry.

Your course may also give you the chance to place your chemistry within another honours subject, such as biology, physics or the environmental and pharmaceutical sciences, or link it to vocational fields such as business and law.

transferable.text: By the end of your honours degree you should be able to use digital tools to find, gather and organise information and data.

By the end of your honours degree you should be able to choose, examine and criticise research papers and other sources so as to keep your knowledge current, learn further and help solve set problems.

By the end of your honours degree you should be able to apply mathematical ideas and tools, such as rearranging equations, calculus and graphical and statistical methods, to chemical problems and data.
By the end of your honours degree you should be able to pick and apply methods for analysing and handling data, which may include coding or scripting, to present, communicate and solve problems.
By the end of your honours degree you should be able to work well with others in a group, contributing constructively and adaptably to shared outputs.
By the end of your honours degree you should be able to communicate well, choosing content, medium and method to suit the audience, purpose and topic.
By the end of your honours degree you should be able to tell apart different kinds of published information and understand how peer review shapes the scientific literature.
By the end of your honours degree you should be able to understand what your own and others' intellectual property is and is worth, and why academic integrity matters.
By the end of your honours degree you should be able to behave professionally, mindful of legal, ethical and social duties, setting an example that reflects well on chemistry and chemists.
By the end of your integrated master's you should be able to devise new ways to tackle advanced problems, at times without full information.
By the end of your integrated master's you should be able to build persuasive arguments and state your position, drawing knowledge and skills together into a convincing case for your ideas.

By the end of your integrated master's you should be able to question and combine varied scientific literature and other information to design methods of investigation and analysis, also beyond your specialism.
By the end of your integrated master's you should be able to build general strategies for problems with more than one answer, including finding the extra information needed.
By the end of your integrated master's you should be able to plan and manage your own work and a group's work well.
By the end of your integrated master's you should be able to show readiness for research, a doctorate or employment at a similar level.

statements.about: representative material and an inclusive setting
statements.paraphrase: The aims that follow should be read as part of giving every chemistry student relevant, representative material and a welcoming, inclusive setting where all feel valued and can come to enjoy the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Read the course aims through an inclusion lens: choose material that is relevant and representative for every student, and build a setting where all feel welcome and valued.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Chemistry degree

statements.paraphrase: Because chemistry is very broad, courses should show that breadth in what they cover and in how they teach, learn and assess; some courses cover the whole field, others let students specialise or combine chemistry with other subjects.

forPractitioner.text: Let the breadth of chemistry show in both the topics covered and the variety of teaching, learning and assessment methods, whether the course is broad, specialist, joint or combined.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Chemistry degree

statements.paraphrase: Practical work is essential to every chemistry course: all graduates will be competent and able to work safely and accurately in a laboratory, and by the final year students work precisely with little supervision, sorting out problems as they come; courses build this in a spiral, from detailed instructions to independence.

forPractitioner.text: Plan practical work as a spiral: detailed instructions and forgiving experiments early, then less support, so that final-year students work precisely with little supervision and every graduate is safe and accurate in the laboratory.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your course you will be able to work safely and accurately in a laboratory, and in your final year you will work precisely with little supervision, solving problems as they come up.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Chemistry degree

statements.about: an inclusive account of chemistry and its uses
statements.paraphrase: Though chemistry rests on objective observation, its history and its uses in society must be presented and taught inclusively; curricula should credit chemists of diverse backgrounds, accept that other cultures bring other insights, let learners explore topics that matter to them and encourage them to weigh both the good and harm that chemical discoveries can do.

forPractitioner.text: Teach the history and applications of chemistry inclusively as a must; as shoulds, credit chemists from diverse backgrounds, give learners room to follow topics tied to their own experience, and ask them to weigh benefits and harms of discoveries.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Chemistry degree

statements.paraphrase: Chemistry is central to solving problems, so courses should inspire chemists to take part in tackling personal, human and global challenges; topics may come from the UN Sustainable Development Goals, and ESD is part of studying chemistry, equipping graduates to devise new answers to complex challenges.

forPractitioner.text: Inspire students to engage with global challenges through chemistry; draw topics where useful from the SDGs, such as health, energy, clean water and the environment, and use the QAA and Advance HE ESD guidance.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Chemistry degree

statements.about: employability: subject skills and wider attributes
statements.paraphrase: All chemistry courses should prepare students for life after graduation in a complex, changing world and for a useful contribution to society; graduates should have both the subject knowledge and professional skills for chemical careers and the wider attributes for careers elsewhere.

forPractitioner.text: Build both subject-specific professional skills and wider attributes into the course, so graduates can work in the chemical sciences or in other sectors; 3.8 lists the wider skills.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should prepare you for work in chemistry and beyond it, giving you both subject expertise and the wider skills employers in other sectors value.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Chemistry degree

statements.paraphrase: Chemistry courses across the UK are designed in many ways, by traditional branches, by synthesis, measurement and application, or around applied fields; whichever lead they take, all courses should include a suitable mix of fundamental theory and application.

forPractitioner.text: Whatever structure the course takes, branches or applications, make sure it combines fundamental theory and application in suitable proportion.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: bachelor's degrees with honours in chemistry
statements.about: what honours degrees provide; the integrated master's
statements.paraphrase: Undergraduates may take a bachelor's degree with honours (FHEQ 6; FQHEIS 10) or an integrated master's with honours (FHEQ 7; FQHEIS 11), each with its own outcomes; bachelor's degrees should give subject knowledge, understanding and skills plus wider transferable skills for many careers, while integrated master's degrees cover both sets of outcomes and go deeper.

forPractitioner.text: Give honours students subject knowledge, understanding and skills together with wider transferable skills; in an integrated master's, meet the honours outcomes and add the depth, specialist knowledge and project work of master's level.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Chemistry degree

statements.paraphrase: Courses may include placements or study abroad, often in the third or fourth year and of varied length and credit; credit-bearing placements should be built into the course so students can link their experience and skills to their academic study.

forPractitioner.text: Where a placement carries credit, integrate it with the rest of the course so students connect what they do on placement with their academic work.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: The academic part of chemistry degree apprenticeships should follow this statement; apprenticeships in general are described in QAA's characteristics statement on higher education in apprenticeships.

forPractitioner.text: Design the academic component of a chemistry degree apprenticeship to the same outcomes as other chemistry degrees, reading the apprenticeships characteristics statement alongside.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Chemistry degree

statements.paraphrase: Equal opportunity means access for people with differing needs and removing needless barriers; chemistry courses must make learning and assessment equally accessible to all, by inclusive design where possible and reasonable adjustment where needed, and learning and assessment should be varied to reflect the subject and widen access.

forPractitioner.text: As a must, design learning and assessment inclusively so they are equally accessible, adding reasonable individual adjustments where needed; as a should, vary the experiences to reflect the subject and widen access.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.paraphrase: Course teams must take care that curricula, teaching, assessments and practical work are built for full accessibility, and that every learner gets support to develop the verbal, spatial, numerical and other skills chemical problems call for.

forPractitioner.text: Check every element, curriculum, pedagogy, assessment and practicals, for full accessibility, and support all learners in the verbal, spatial and numerical skills chemistry needs.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: progression from defined to open problems
statements.paraphrase: Courses should be designed to foster academic and personal growth: students first use simple concepts on well-defined problems, then link harder concepts to tackle ill-defined, open problems, and on graduating will have the range of knowledge, experience and skills for a career in chemistry or elsewhere.

forPractitioner.text: Sequence the course so students move from simple concepts and well-defined problems to complex concepts and open-ended ones, ending with the competence a chemistry career needs.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should take you from using simple ideas on clear-cut problems to connecting harder ideas on open-ended ones, so that you finish ready for a career in chemistry or another field.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Chemistry degree

statements.paraphrase: Strategies for progression should take account of how varied students' prior experience is and how hard transition can be.

forPractitioner.text: Plan induction and early teaching around the range of prior experience in the cohort and the difficulty of moving into higher education.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider or course team; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Chemistry degree
